slides: Welcome back, and now a new topic, averages.

slides.say: Average questions come up in almost every exam. They use a few simple ideas. Once you know them, these questions are quick.
On the exam, it usually just says the average. It's the average you know from school.
An average is one number that describes the middle of a group of numbers. So let's see what the middle means.
Let's start with the easy case, numbers that are symmetric. Take sixteen and thirty. Where's the middle?
Sixteen plus seven is twenty-three. And twenty-three plus seven is thirty.
So twenty-three is seven above sixteen, and seven below thirty. It's exactly in the middle.
So the average of sixteen and thirty is twenty-three.
Now four numbers. Six, ten, fourteen and eighteen.
Six and eighteen are a pair. Their middle is twelve, because six plus six is twelve, and twelve plus six is eighteen.
Ten and fourteen are also a pair. Ten plus two is twelve, and twelve plus two is fourteen. So their middle is twelve too.
Every pair has the same middle, twelve. So the average of all four numbers is twelve.
at: Every pair has the same middle

slides.say: So when the numbers are symmetric, the average is the middle. We don't need to calculate.
at: So when the numbers are symmetric

slides.say: On the exam, symmetric numbers often come as evenly spaced numbers. That means each number is the same step above the one before.
For example, three, seven, eleven, fifteen and nineteen.
Each one is four more than the one before.
Evenly spaced numbers are symmetric around the middle one. Three and nineteen are a pair. Seven and fifteen are a pair. And eleven is in the middle.
at: Three and nineteen are a pair
Seven and fifteen are a pair

slides.say: So the average is the middle number, eleven.
at: So the average is the middle number

slides.say: There's another way. Take the first number and the last number, and find their middle.
Three plus nineteen is twenty-two. And twenty-two divided by two is eleven. The same eleven.
Numbers in a row are evenly spaced too. For example, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two, and so on up to thirty. Each step is one.
So the average is the first plus the last, divided by two. Twenty plus thirty is fifty. Fifty divided by two is twenty-five.
And what if there's no single middle number? Take four, six, eight and ten. That's four numbers, so there are two middle numbers, six and eight.
Then the average is halfway between them, seven.
And the first plus the last works here too. Four plus ten is fourteen, and fourteen divided by two is seven.
Now let's add a number to a group. Take three, five and seven. The average is five, the middle.
And five is also one of the numbers. It sits right on the middle.
Now let's add another five. What's the average of three, five, five and seven? Three and seven are still a pair around five. So the average is still five.
at: What's the average of three, five, five
So the average is still five

slides.say: Why? A number that is equal to the average sits on the middle. It doesn't pull the middle up, and it doesn't pull it down.
So here's our first rule. If we add or remove a number equal to the average, the average doesn't change.
For example, four numbers have an average of ten. We add a fifth number, ten. The average stays ten.
at: four numbers have an average of ten

slides.say: But if we add twelve, that's more than the average. So the average goes up. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
